chunks: "I put power planes on inner layers, directly next to a ground plane, with as thin a dielectric between them as the stackup allows.
On a four-layer board that's layer 3, right under the ground on layer 2.
On a six-layer, I'd put power on layer 4, next to the ground on layer 5, so the power and ground planes are neighbours.

The reason is that a power plane and ground plane close together act like a big parallel-plate capacitor, with very little inductance, and that helps decoupling at high frequency, where discrete capacitors stop helping because of their own inductance.
It also keeps the loop for the current feeding the chips small.
I avoid putting full power planes on the outer layers because that's where the components and the routing are, and I'd rather use pours there for high-current rails.

If there are several rails, I split the power layer into islands, put the biggest or the one with the fastest load closest to the chip it feeds, and keep fast signals from crossing the gaps, since a signal referenced to a split plane loses its return path.
And I still use decoupling capacitors, because at 50 or 100 megahertz and below they're doing most of the work."
